idiom_name: value semantics (structs, copy-on-write collections) replaces the classic clone; `NSCopying.copy(with:)` for reference types
implementation_notes: For value types the pattern is unnecessary: structs and enums are copied on assignment and when passed as arguments, and the standard collections are copy-on-write, so 'copy through an interface' normally becomes 'pass the value'. Where reference semantics are required (classes needing identity), Foundation's `NSCopying` - a single `copy(with:)` method, usually invoked through the `copy()` convenience - is the classic clone, and a hierarchy can also expose its own `init(copying:)` initializer or `clone()` method returning the base type. The recommended move is therefore structural: model the data as a struct and the class as an identity-bearing service, and implement `copy(with:)` only when a reference type genuinely has to be duplicated through a base-class reference.
pitfalls: `NSCopying` requires inheriting `NSObject`, declares `copy(with:) -> Any`, so every call site force-casts (`as! Document`); a subclass that inherits the conformance without overriding it returns a copy of the superclass state (silent data loss).

The `@NSCopying` attribute does not deep-copy in initializers - property setters (and therefore the copying behaviour) are not called during initialization, so a 'copied' reference can still be shared unless you assign the copy explicitly.
A struct is only value-semantic while all its stored properties are value types or deliberately copy-on-write: a struct holding a class reference shares that object with every copy.
`copy(with:)` is by contract shallow unless you make it deep - reference-typed properties and collections of class instances must be copied explicitly, or original and copy mutate each other.
